title: Why do we suffer?
hook: every tradition asks it, and each answers differently

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Diogenes Laertius, who records Zeno's two ears and one mouth. Your line was listen first: each answer in its own house.

A man blind from birth is sitting by the road. A teacher and his students walk past, and the students ask out loud, right there: whose fault is this? Did this man do something wrong, or did his parents? It's an old question, and a hard one to hear about yourself. When something terrible happens, the nearest reason to hand is often blame. Today, the year's first great question: why do we suffer? Four answers, each in its own voice.
screen: `A MAN BLIND FROM BIRTH.` → `WHOSE FAULT IS THIS?` → `THE FIRST GREAT QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the Gospel of John. The disciples ask, "Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" And Jesus answers, "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." Then he heals him. There's a lot in the rest of that answer, but its first word is plain: neither. The shortcut to blame is closed. Second, the Qur'an. In the second surah, God says that people will be tried with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops, and then: give glad tidings to the steadfast. Hardship, in this answer, is a test, and the response it asks for is steadfastness. The Arabic word behind it is sabr, patience that holds. Third, the Buddha. In his first teaching he names suffering, then where it comes from: a craving, a thirst, always reaching for more and for something else. We'll spend the coming days inside that answer. Fourth, the Stoic Epictetus. His Handbook says that what troubles people isn't the things that happen, but their judgments about them. Death isn't terrible, or Socrates would have thought so; the terror is in our opinion of death. A test met with patience. A thirst. A judgment. And a story where blame is refused, and the story moves on to healing. They don't line up into one tidy reply, and this year won't force them to. Each speaks for itself.
screen: `WHO SINNED? NEITHER.` · `THE QUR'AN: TRIED, AND STEADFAST.` · `THE BUDDHA: A THIRST.` · `EPICTETUS: OUR JUDGMENTS.` · then, large: `EACH ANSWERS DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: Let one real weight you carry come to mind, an ache, a worry, a loss; it needn't be the heaviest, and it needn't have words yet. Then let the four answers pass by it like visitors at a bedside: a test, a thirst, a judgment, neither he nor his parents. You don't have to agree with any of them; just notice which visitor you'd let stay a little longer.
Sabr, the Arabic word for patience that holds steady under trial, the response the Qur'an asks of the steadfast. Today's word.
Your line: each answers differently. One question, four voices, no blending. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Some people bring suffering to their own tradition's texts and teachers: Christians to the Gospels and prayer, Muslims to the Qur'an and the practice of patience, Buddhists to the four noble truths, students of Stoicism to the Handbook.

chat.says: In that story about the blind man, whose fault did Jesus say it was?
options: Neither his nor his parents'; Jesus closed the shortcut to blame.
His parents'; Jesus said he was paying for their old sins.
His own; Jesus said he had sinned before he was born.
chat.meaning: Jesus answers, "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents," refusing blame, and then the story moves on to healing.

sabr.meaning: Arabic for patience that holds steady under trial

Epictetus.meaning: a once-enslaved Stoic teacher; his Handbook is a short guide

notes: Audit (80-day test): practice no longer has the listener name the suffering 'in a few plain words', which was day 700's whole practice (name it first); here it is held without words, and the naming is left to tomorrow.

Editor: John 9:2 has the disciples (plural) ask, so 'one of the students' and 'within earshot' were cut; John's answer summarized as 'blame refused' / 'neither he nor his parents' rather than 'not your fault', which left out the rest of 9:3; 'asked by every tradition' and 'people in many traditions' softened.

Qur'an 2:155 paraphrased closely after Pickthall ('We shall try you with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops; but give glad tidings to the steadfast'), with quoted: null to be safe. A Keeper may prefer to quote Pickthall exactly.
Original: sabr (صبر); the word in 2:155 is as-sabirin, from the same root. Confirm the note.
Enchiridion 5 paraphrased (the Socrates example); the familiar Long 1877 line was used on day 285, so it is not quoted again here.
